name: Colosseum
label: Colosseum
camera_source: OpenStreetMap viewpoint 'Colosseo' (node/5978649686). Moved 78 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 180 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1834818: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Colosseum' (229 m across).
notes: 'colosseum' alone (512,000) includes other venues called Colosseum; 'colosseum rome' alone is 49,800. Counting only 'colosseum rome' would put it 8th; the true figure lies between the two (unmeasured).

text.description:
The Colosseum is the great oval amphitheatre in the middle of Rome, and it is the largest standing amphitheatre in the world. Work began in AD 72 under the Emperor Vespasian and finished in AD 80 under his successor and heir, Titus, with more changes made later under Domitian. It was built on the flat ground of a low valley, where Nero's artificial lake had been filled in. The name is thought to come from a huge bronze statue of Nero that once stood close by. It could hold tens of thousands of spectators, and today you see the ruined outer wall, with its rows of arches, against the sky.

It photographs well because the shape is instantly recognisable and the repeating arches give a strong pattern. The broken edge of the wall adds drama, and the stone changes colour as the light changes. Because the building is so large, the main challenge is fitting it in without tilting the phone upwards, which makes the walls lean inwards. Stand back where you can, keep the phone level, and use the gridlines to line up the arches. For detail shots, move in or use the zoom to pick out a single bay of arches, the worn stone or a patch of sky through a gap. Expect other visitors in the frame, so a few quick shots as people move through will help. Look around the whole outside as well, because the ruined and the more complete sections give very different pictures.
text.geographic_location: The Colosseum stands in the centre of Rome, just east of the Roman Forum, in the low ground between the Caelian, Esquiline and Palatine Hills. Colosseo station (Metro line B, with tram 3 and tram 8) and the Colosseo/Salvi N. tram stop are right beside it.
text.directions_text: From Colosseo station (Metro line B, with tram 3 and tram 8), the Colosseum is about 92 m to the south, about 1 minute on foot. From Colosseo – Fori Imperiali (Metro line C), it lies to the south-east, about 4 minutes on foot. If you arrive by tram 3 or tram 8 at Colosseo/Salvi N., the building is to the west, about 2 minutes on foot; from the Parco Celio stop (also tram 3 and tram 8) it is to the north, about 5 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the long curve of the walls in from close range, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of the arches and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Via Nicola Salvi (raised section near the Colosseo metro exit, northern side). The Colosseum's most intact outer curve and facade, filling the frame from a slight height above the piazza.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. Put the curve of the arches along one of the lines, and leave a little sky above the top edge. For a second shot, zoom in on a single row of arches so the pattern fills the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the stone to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white. If you want the whole curve of the building, try panorama mode and move the phone slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and warmer stone colour, and often fewer people. After dark, if the building is lit, night mode can give a good result; hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The area around the Colosseum is a busy public space, but entry to the interior is likely to be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Trevi Fountain
label: Trevi Fountain
camera_source: Commons cluster (26 photos). Moved 4 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 20 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/13448560: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Trevi Fountain' (61 m across).

text.description:
The Trevi Fountain is a huge Baroque fountain built into the back of a palace, so it feels more like a stage set than a monument. It stands 26.3 metres high and 49.15 metres wide, and is described as the largest Baroque fountain in the world. Nicola Salvi designed it, and Giuseppe Pannini finished it in 1762. The backdrop is the Palazzo Poli, given a new façade with tall Corinthian pilasters and a triumphal-arch centrepiece. In the central niche stands Oceanus on a shell chariot, guided by tritons and sea-horses, with rockwork and water spilling forward into the small square.

It photographs well because there is so much to look at. The carved stone is a pale travertine, and the free-standing columns around the central niche create strong light and shade. The fountain was also restored between 2014 and 2015, when more than 100 LED lights were added to improve its night-time lighting, so the evening view is worth a try.

The main challenge for a phone is the size of the fountain compared with the space in front of it. Once you have that, switch to the zoom for close-ups of Oceanus and the sculpted figures. Expect people in the foreground. Treat them as scale, or wait for a gap and take a burst of shots.
text.geographic_location: The fountain is in the Trevi district in the centre of Rome, set against the Palazzo Poli where Via de' Crocicchi, Via Poli and Via delle Muratte meet.
text.directions_text: By Metro (Metropolitana), Barberini on Metro line A is the closest station: the fountain is to the south-west, about 9 minutes on foot. Spagna, also on Metro line A, is about 11 minutes on foot, with the fountain to the south. From the tram 8 stop at Venezia, the fountain lies to the north, about 11 minutes on foot. The streets around the fountain are narrow, so follow the signs and the crowd for the last stretch. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole façade and the basin in one frame. Switch to 1x for a tidier, less stretched view, then use 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of Oceanus and the horses.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. This is far enough back to take in the full width, but in the main square people often fill the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the central niche with the middle vertical line so the symmetry looks right. Keep the phone level, since tilting it will make the palace columns lean. Let the water and a few people fill the bottom of the frame to give a sense of size. For detail shots, use the zoom to isolate Oceanus, the tritons or the rockwork rather than moving closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright travertine and water keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady. A Live Photo can capture the moving water, but a normal shot is better for the carvings.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is likely to be quieter. In the evening, the fountain's LED lighting gives a dramatic look, so try a few shots at dusk and after dark.

text.access_note: The fountain stands in an open square, but a city ticketing system for non-residents to approach the water was introduced in February 2026, so check the official site before you go.

name: St Peter's Basilica and Square
label: St Peter's
camera_source: Commons cluster (146 photos). Moved 106 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 290 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/244159210: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint Peter's Basilica' (268 m across).
notes: IN VATICAN CITY (pilot map 9). Kept because visitors search it as part of Rome: your decision. UK figure for 'st peter's square' (74,000) is probably Manchester's St Peter's Square, so the square's figure is not used.

text.description:
St Peter's is the great Renaissance church of Vatican City, and its dome is the high point of Rome's skyline. In front of it, Bernini's square opens out like a pair of arms. Two sweeping Tuscan colonnades, four columns deep, enclose an oval space with an Egyptian obelisk at its centre and a fountain on each side. Bernini designed the square between 1667 and 1676, and the obelisk had been raised on the spot in 1586. The present basilica was begun in 1506 and finished in 1626. It is counted as the largest church in the world by interior measure, and its dome is among the biggest anywhere.

It photographs well because the scale is easy to read. The wide façade, the dome rising behind it and the curving colonnades all line up along one axis, and the trapezoid-shaped approach gives the view real depth. People crossing the square give a quick sense of size.

From there the whole group of dome, façade and square fits in one frame. For a close-up of the colonnades or the façade details, walk into the square. Papal ceremonies here can draw between 15,000 and over 80,000 people, so expect the square to be very busy on those days. The basilica is a working church, so check the official site for entry rules before you go.
text.geographic_location: St Peter's Basilica and Square sit in Vatican City, an independent enclave inside Rome, on the west side of the River Tiber.
text.directions_text: Take the Metro: on Metro line A, Cipro is the nearest station. From there the basilica is to the south-east, about 12 minutes on foot. From Ottaviano, also on Metro line A, the basilica is to the south-west, about 15 minutes on foot. If you prefer a tram, tram 19 stops at Risorgimento/S. Pietro, and the basilica is south-west of the stop, about 9 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene of dome, façade and colonnades. From where you stand, use 2x or 3x to bring the dome and façade closer without cropping the picture yourself. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) once you are inside the square and want the curve of the colonnades.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ponte Umberto I. Looking toward the Vatican along the Tiber, with Ponte Sant'Angelo leading the eye to the basilica's dome. For the colonnade shots, walk west into the square, roughly 5 minutes on foot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the dome on the central vertical line, so the façade sits level and symmetrical. In the square, use the 0.5x lens and stand near the centre, with the obelisk as a middle anchor. Keep the phone level, because ultra-wide lenses make the columns lean if you tilt them. Let a few people walk through the foreground to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the stone keeps its texture. Use Live Photos if you like a moving crowd, and try panorama only in the square, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually gives softer light and fewer people, and the façade is likely to be lit from the front. Dusk is good for night mode, with the dome standing out against the darkening sky.

text.access_note: The basilica is a place of worship in Vatican City, so entry and any dress or security rules may apply; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The basilica façade faces east, so morning light falls on it from the stand-here side.
Early mornings are usually quieter than the middle of the day.
Dusk and night views of the lit dome work well with a phone's night mode.
The basilica may have security checks, queues and a dress code for entry.
Ultra-wide lenses can make vertical lines lean if the phone is tilted.

name: Spanish Steps and Piazza di Spagna
label: Spanish Steps
camera_source: Commons cluster (60 photos). Moved 39 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 45 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/134400816: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Spanish Steps' (108 m across).

text.description: The Spanish Steps are a wide stone stairway of 135 steps that climbs from Piazza di Spagna up to the church of Trinità dei Monti. They are a popular photo spot, ranked 4th on the Rome shot map. The slope is about 29 metres high, and the stairway opens and narrows in curves and landings, which gives your pictures strong shapes: sweeping lines, a twin-towered church at the top and plenty of people for scale. The design was chosen in a competition in 1717 and won by Francesco de Sanctis. The steps were restored in 2015–2016 (reopened 21 September 2016). At the foot of the steps, in the square, is the Fontana della Barcaccia, the 'fountain of the longboat', built in 1627-29. It makes a good foreground for photos looking up the stairs. Keats's house, now a museum, stands at the right-hand corner as you face the steps. Try the full view from the piazza first, then a closer frame of the fountain with the steps behind it. Climb up for a view back over the square and rooftops. In spring the steps may be lined with pots of azaleas, which add colour. The steps are usually crowded, so be patient and shoot between groups. Local rules restrict sitting and eating on the steps, so keep your photo stops short and don't block the stairs.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Rome, at the Spanish Steps (about 41.90599° N, 12.48278° E), where Piazza di Spagna meets the foot of the stairway to Trinità dei Monti on the edge of the Pincio hill. The square is lined with luxury shops, and Via dei Condotti runs nearby.
text.directions_text: The nearest Metro station is Spagna (Metro line A): from there walk south-west for about 3 minutes on foot to reach the steps. From Barberini (Metro line A), walk north-west for about 9 minutes on foot. If you are coming by tram, Flaminio (MA) is served by tram 2, and the steps are about 15 minutes on foot to the south-east; Galleria Arte Moderna is served by tram 3, and the steps are about 20 minutes on foot to the south. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole stairway, church and fountain in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use 2x-5x zoom, if your phone has it, to pick out the church facade or the fountain's detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza di Spagna (foot of the steps, beside the Fontana della Barcaccia). The full staircase rising toward the Trinità dei Monti church, with the boat-shaped fountain in the foreground. Step closer for the fountain, or walk up the steps for a view back over the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals straight. Put the Barcaccia fountain low in the frame and let the steps rise behind it. Wait for gaps in the crowd, or use the people for scale. Try one shot in portrait orientation to catch the full climb up to the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the scene to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is washing out. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing to avoid blur.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is likely to be calmer for photos. Late afternoon and evening are good for softer light and for night shots with the lights on.

text.access_note: The steps and the piazza are an open public space, but local rules restrict sitting and eating on the steps and access can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Piazza Navona
label: Piazza Navona
camera_source: Commons cluster (166 photos).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4247138: 'Fountain of the Four Rivers', the best-known feature inside 'Piazza Navona' (269 m across).

text.description:
Piazza Navona is a long, oval-shaped public square in the centre of Rome. Its shape is no accident: it sits on the Stadium of Domitian, which was begun in 80 AD, and the open space still follows the outline of the old running track. Only a few remains of the stadium survive today. The look you see now comes mostly from the 17th century, when the square became a showcase for Baroque design under Pope Innocent X. In the middle is Bernini's Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi (1651), topped by an obelisk, and facing it is the church of Sant'Agnese in Agone, with contributions from Borromini and others. There are two more fountains: the Fontana del Moro at the southern end and the Fountain of Neptune at the northern end.

It photographs well because everything is packed into one open space. You get sculpture, water, curving church fronts and warm-coloured buildings in a single sweep. The long oval also gives you plenty of room to step back and fit a whole scene in. On a phone, the ultra-wide lens is your best friend here, with the zoom for close-ups of the carved figures. A Christmas market fills the square from the first week of December to the first week of January, which adds atmosphere but also stalls and crowds in your frame. Expect people in most shots at any time of year, so use them as part of the scene rather than fighting them.
text.geographic_location: Piazza Navona is in Rome's historic centre, and the map marks the Fountain of the Four Rivers in the middle of the square. Campo de' Fiori, where the market moved in 1869, is nearby.
text.directions_text: From the Arenula/Cairoli stop (tram 8), the square is to the north, about 10 minutes on foot. From Spagna (Metro line A), the square lies to the south-west, about 21 minutes on foot. Barberini (Metro line A) is a little further, also to the south-west, about 23 minutes on foot. Once you reach the square, walk to the phone icon on the map, described below. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full width of the piazza and the fountain together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the church front. Use 2x-3x zoom, if your phone has it, for the carved figures and the obelisk without leaning over the crowds.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. From there you look south, towards the southern end of the piazza where the Fontana del Moro is. You then have the open oval of the square stretching away in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the buildings upright by lining the vertical edges up with the grid. Let the fountain take up one third of the frame and leave the rest for the building fronts and sky. Crouching a little lowers the viewpoint, which makes heads blend into the crowd and the fountain stand taller.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework or the fountain to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the bright sky and sunlit stone don't wash out. Try a Live Photo of the fountains so you can pick a frame with the water caught nicely. Use panorama, held steady and moved slowly, to capture the oval shape.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people and softer light. In the evening, if the fountains and buildings are lit, switch on night mode and hold the phone still against your body for sharper shots.

text.access_note: The piazza is a public open space; if you plan to go inside Sant'Agnese in Agone or any nearby museum, check the official site before you go.

name: Pantheon
label: Pantheon
camera_source: Commons cluster (132 photos). Moved 39 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 65 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3374342: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pantheon' (103 m across).
notes: Only 'pantheon rome' counted ('pantheon' alone also means the Paris Pantheon).

text.description: The Pantheon is an ancient Roman temple that has been a church for well over a thousand years. The first building here was commissioned by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa under Augustus. After it burnt down, Hadrian's rebuilding was completed and probably dedicated around AD 126. Since AD 609 it has been a Catholic church, which is a large part of why it survives so well. It photographs well because its shape is easy to read: a deep porch with eight huge granite columns across the front, and a plain round drum behind. The square in front is called Piazza della Rotonda, and it gives you room to step back. Inside, the coffered concrete dome has a central opening to the sky. The height to that opening and the width of the interior circle are both 43 metres. The dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. For a phone, the key problem is fitting the columns and pediment into one frame without tilting the phone up too far. Then move in for tighter shots of the column rows. Expect other visitors in most frames, so wait for small gaps or use them as part of the picture.
text.geographic_location: The Pantheon is in the historic centre of Rome, on Piazza della Rotonda, in the Campus Martius area. It is about 8 minutes on foot from the Venezia tram stop (tram 8), with the Pantheon to the north-west of the stop.
text.directions_text: The easiest approach is tram 8 to Venezia, then walk north-west for about 8 minutes on foot (513 m). Tram 8 also stops at Arenula/Cairoli, about 9 minutes on foot, with the Pantheon to the north. From Metro line A, Spagna and Barberini are both about 18 minutes on foot, with the Pantheon to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) from where you stand to take in the whole portico and pediment. Switch to 2x or 3x if your phone has it, for the columns and the inscription band. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move much closer or want a sweeping shot of the square, and keep the building centred so the edges don't stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza della Rotonda (far side of the Fontana del Pantheon, facing the facade). A symmetrical, front-on view of the Pantheon's portico with the obelisk fountain in the foreground. This puts you roughly in line with the centre of the facade, so the columns look balanced.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the central pair of columns with the middle vertical line. Keep the phone level, with the horizon line of the pediment parallel to a horizontal gridline, to avoid converging verticals. Leave a little space at the bottom of the frame for the people in front of the columns, which shows how big the building is.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework of the portico to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and pale stone don't wash out. If people keep walking through the shot, try a Live Photo and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the evening usually means fewer people in the square. Check how the light falls on the front on the day, as the facade faces north and can look flat or shaded.

text.access_note: The Pantheon is a state-managed monument and a working church, so check the official site before you go for entry rules and any dress requirements.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning and evening are usually less crowded at the Pantheon.
A north-facing facade can look flat or partly shaded depending on the time of day.
Standing back and keeping the phone level reduces converging verticals in photos of tall buildings.
A working church may have a dress code and restrictions on photography inside.

name: Trastevere: Piazza di Santa Maria and the lanes
label: Trastevere
camera_source: Commons cluster (66 photos). Moved 28 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 60 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/51368975: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilica di Santa Maria in Trastevere' (85 m across).
notes: A district, missed by the first pull (districts were filtered out); measured in the second pull.

text.description: The square in front of Santa Maria in Trastevere is the sort of place where you can lift your phone almost anywhere and get something pleasant. The piazza is built around an octagonal fountain, with the front of Santa Maria in Trastevere closing one side and lanes running off in several directions. The church is one of the oldest in Rome. It was largely rebuilt in 1140-43 under Pope Innocent II, and the façade was restored in 1702 by Carlo Fontana. Fontana also restored the fountain, which already appears on a map of 1472. Look up at the Romanesque bell tower, where a niche near the top holds a 13th-century mosaic of the Madonna and Child by Pietro Cavallini. It is a good detail to zoom in on. The name Trastevere comes from the Latin for 'beyond the Tiber', and the district kept narrow, winding streets for centuries. Those streets are why the lanes around the square suit snapshots: stone walls, doorways and cobbles (sampietrini) give you texture and a feeling of depth. Start with a wide shot of the square, then move to the fountain with the church behind it, then step into a side lane for a tighter, more intimate frame. Expect other visitors in your pictures, so wait a few seconds for gaps.
text.geographic_location: In the Trastevere district (the 13th rione of Rome), on the west bank of the Tiber. The spot is the square in front of the basilica of Santa Maria in Trastevere and the lanes around it.
text.directions_text: The easiest approach is tram 8 to Trastevere/Mastai, then about 6 minutes on foot (356 m) with the square to the north-west. From the Belli stop on tram 8 it is about 7 minutes on foot (403 m), heading west. If you are coming by Metro, Circo Massimo (Metro line B) is the nearest station, but it is about 1.7 km away, about 27 minutes on foot, heading north-west, so the tram is the more practical choice. The phone icon on the map is about 60 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole square, the fountain and the church front together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for lane scenes. Use 2x-5x, depending on your phone, to pick out the mosaic high on the bell tower without walking closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 60 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. It gives you a clear view across the open square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the fountain on a lower third line with the church front rising behind it. Keep the vertical lines of the building straight by holding the phone level. In a lane, use the walls on either side as leading lines towards a bright opening at the far end.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church front to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so bright stonework and sky don't wash out. For the tower mosaic, zoom in and steady your elbows against your body to keep it sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people in the square. In the evening the lights come on and night mode can handle the lanes, though it will be busier.

text.access_note: The square and lanes are open public space, but the basilica is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and dress expectations.

name: Roman Forum and Arch of Titus
label: Roman Forum
camera_source: OpenStreetMap viewpoint 'Torre del Tabularium' (node/1987788474).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1841080: large area 'Roman Forum' (706 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Arch of Titus (17,210) merged: it stands inside the Forum. Camera: Capitoline terraces above the Forum (OSM viewpoints Torre del Tabularium, Forum Romanum view).

text.description:
The Roman Forum was the centre of daily life in ancient Rome: a public square where processions, speeches, trials and business all happened. It sits in the small valley between the Palatine and Capitoline hills. Today it is a spread of broken columns, temple bases and arches, and that makes it a good phone subject. There are plenty of strong shapes, and the sightlines are long.

By imperial times the open square had shrunk to roughly 130 by 50 metres, hemmed in by big public buildings. It runs north-west to south-east, and its final travertine paving, laid under Augustus, can still be seen. At the south-east end stands the Arch of Titus, built around 81 AD after the death of Titus. It is about 15.4 metres tall and 13.5 metres wide, and its panels show the triumphal procession of 71 AD. The sources say the Forum draws 4.5 million or more visitors a year, so expect other people in your frame.

For a simple, strong shot, stand at the marked viewpoint and look towards the Forum. Use the ultra-wide camera for the scattered ruins and the sky, then zoom in on single columns or the arch. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines, as the ruins are full of vertical lines that look odd if tilted. Take a few shots at each setting, because crowds move through quickly and you can pick the cleanest frame afterwards.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Rome, in the valley between the Palatine and Capitoline hills. The Arch of Titus marks its south-east end, not far from the Colosseum.
text.directions_text: Start from the Metro line C station Colosseo – Fori Imperiali: the Forum is about 7 minutes on foot, to the west. From the Metro line B, tram 3 and tram 8 station Colosseo, it is about 10 minutes on foot, also to the west. From the tram 8 stop Venezia, it is about 8 minutes on foot, to the south-east. From the tram 3 and tram 8 stop Parco Celio, it is about 11 minutes on foot, to the north-west. Follow the signs and the flow of visitors, and check the official site for where you can enter. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the wide spread of ruins, then use 1x for general views. Switch to the 2x-5x zoom, depending on your phone, for the Arch of Titus and details of columns and carvings.

name: Castel Sant'Angelo and Ponte Sant'Angelo
label: Castel Sant'Angelo
camera_source: OpenStreetMap viewpoint 'Punto panoramico di Ponte Umberto I' (node/4978038129). Moved 62 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 430 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/8035487: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Castle of the Holy Angel' (178 m across).
notes: Camera: the classic view from Ponte Umberto I (OSM viewpoint).

text.description: Castel Sant'Angelo is a big round fortress beside the Tiber, and the pedestrian Ponte Sant'Angelo leads straight up to it. That alignment is why the pair photographs so well: the bridge gives you a line of arches and statues, and the castle fills the end of the view. Emperor Hadrian had the castle built as a family tomb between 134 and 139 AD, and the bridge was finished in 134 AD to reach it. Later the popes turned the tomb into a fortress, and it was decommissioned as a fortress in 1901 and is now a museum. A bronze statue of Saint Michael on the top dates from 1753. The bridge has five arches, three of them Roman, and it carries Baroque angels holding instruments of the Passion, part of a scheme led by Bernini. Because the bridge is closed to traffic, you can stop and compose a shot without worrying about cars. For the classic view of the whole group, go to the Ponte Umberto I viewpoint, about 430 m east of the castle, and look west along the river. For close detail, walk onto Ponte Sant'Angelo and shoot the angels with the castle behind them. Expect plenty of other people on the bridge, so wait for a gap or shoot upwards at the statues against the sky. Keep your phone's gridlines on to hold the bridge parapet level, and check that the castle's round shape is not leaning.
text.geographic_location: In the Borgo district on the right (northern) bank of the Tiber, just across the river from the historic centre. The castle stands beside the Parco Adriano gardens, and the bridge links it to the Ponte district on the opposite bank.
text.directions_text: From the Risorgimento/S. Pietro stop (tram 19), head south-east for about 12 minutes on foot to reach the castle. From Metro line A at Lepanto, the castle lies to the south, about 15 minutes on foot; from Ottaviano (Metro line A), it lies to the south-east, about 16 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) from the Ponte Umberto I viewpoint for the whole scene. Switch to 2x or 3x if your phone has a zoom lens, which brings the castle and bridge closer together in the frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the bridge itself to fit the angels, the parapet and the castle into one shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ponte Umberto I. Ponte Sant'Angelo in the foreground with Castel Sant'Angelo beyond it and St. Peter's Basilica's dome in the distance, all framed over the Tiber. Stand at the parapet and look along the river with the bridge and castle ahead of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place Ponte Sant'Angelo's arches in the lower half and let the castle's round tower sit just off-centre. From the bridge itself, stand close to a statue and shoot along the row of angels, so the castle sits at the end of the line. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the castle to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows on the parapet to keep the phone still. Avoid panorama here unless the bridge is quiet, because people walking through will show up as ghosts.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter on the bridge. Late afternoon and the hour after sunset suit the view from Ponte Umberto I, as the light is softer and the castle may be lit up.

text.access_note: Ponte Sant'Angelo is a pedestrian bridge open to everyone, while the castle is a museum, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Circus Maximus
label: Circus Maximus
camera_source: OpenStreetMap viewpoint 'Belvedere Romolo E Remo' (node/393180368). Moved 91 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 65 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/11384819: large area 'Circus Maximus' (684 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Google gives 'circus maximus' and 'circus maximus rome' the same figure (merged), so some searches are probably for the Travis Scott song and film of that name: figure doubtful.

text.description:
The Circus Maximus was ancient Rome's great chariot-racing stadium. It sits in the valley between the Aventine and Palatine hills. Today it is a long, open public park, so it photographs differently from the Colosseum: there is no grand facade, just a huge stretch of grass with hills and trees on either side. That emptiness is the point. It gives you a real sense of scale, and a few people walking across the grass make the size easy to read.

Its ancient size was about 621 m long and 118 m wide, with room for more than 150,000 spectators. It was the first and largest stadium in ancient Rome. The last known races were held there in 549.

It is about 65 m west of the subject, so you look east across the site. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) camera to take in the full length of the grass, then switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched version. If your phone has a 2x-5x zoom, use it to pick out a single group of walkers or a line of trees. Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level, because on such a flat scene a tilted horizon is very noticeable. Lower the exposure slightly if the sky is bright, so it does not wash out.
text.geographic_location: The Circus Maximus lies in central Rome, in the long valley between the Aventine and Palatine hills, south-west of the Colosseum. It is now an open public park.
text.directions_text: The nearest stops are the tram stops Aventino/Circo Massimo (MB) and Aventino/Circo Massimo (tram 3 and tram 8). From either one, the subject is about 335 m to the north-west, about 5 minutes on foot. From Metro line B, get off at Circo Massimo. The subject is about 340 m to the north-west, about 6 minutes on foot. From Colosseo – Fori Imperiali (Metro line C), head south-west for about 741 m, which is about 12 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to show the full length of the grass. Switch to 1x for a more natural look. Use 2x-5x zoom, if your phone has it, for details such as walkers, trees or the far end of the park.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (southern edge, above the track, near the Palace of the Emperors ruins). The whole length of the Circus Maximus track looking straight down from the Palatine's southern edge, with the imperial palace ruins framing the top of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower third line, keeping it level. Include a few people or a path in the foreground so the scale is clear. For a calmer shot, hold the phone at chest height and keep the sides of the frame free of clutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the middle of the park, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks too bright. Try panorama mode for the long view, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and longer shadows across the grass. Midday sun can look flat and harsh.

text.access_note: The site is a public park, but access can change on event days, so check the official site before you go.

name: Palatine Hill
label: Palatine Hill
camera_source: Commons cluster (37 photos): from the Roman Forum looking up at the Palatine.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/365475871: the OpenStreetMap point 'Palatine Hill'.

text.description:
The Palatine is the centremost of Rome's seven hills and one of the oldest parts of the city. It has been called "the first nucleus of the Roman Empire". Excavations show people living here from the 10th century BC. Under the Republic wealthy Romans built their houses on it, and from 27 BC Augustus built his palace here. After that the hill became largely the preserve of emperors. The remains of the palaces of Augustus, Tiberius and Domitian can still be seen. Today it is mostly a large open-air museum, and the Palatine Museum sits in the surviving part of the old Villa Mattei.

The best-known view comes from the Roman Forum, looking up at the hill. The ancient ground drops away in front of you, and the hill rises behind it with ruined walls and greenery along its edge. That layering of foreground ruins, then slope, then sky gives a phone photo a clear sense of scale and depth. The hill is big and spread out, so you will not fit all of it in. Pick one stretch of the slope and frame it with some of the Forum in front.

Take a few frames from the same spot at different zoom levels. A wide shot shows the setting, and a closer one picks out the textures of the old brickwork. Check the official site for current access rules before you go, as parts of the Forum and Palatine area are usually managed as an archaeological site.
text.geographic_location: The Palatine Hill sits in the historic centre of Rome, immediately south of the Roman Forum.
text.directions_text: Start at Colosseo – Fori Imperiali (Metro line C). The Palatine is to the south-west, about 6 minutes on foot. From Colosseo (Metro line B) it is also to the south-west, about 8 minutes on foot. If you arrive by tram 3 or tram 8, get off at Parco Celio, where the hill lies to the north-west, about 6 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 110 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the slope. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the Forum ruins in front and plenty of sky above. Use 2x-3x, or higher if your phone has it, to pick out details along the top of the hill.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 110 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Keep it ahead of you and let some ruins fill the lower part of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the hill's edge on the upper third line, with Forum stones or columns along the bottom. Keep the phone level so the horizon and walls do not lean. Take one wide shot for the setting and one zoomed shot of a single stretch of wall or terrace.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the ruins to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky looks washed out. If the hill is lit from behind, this keeps the details visible. Live Photos are optional and are best skipped in a crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, more directional light. At midday, looking south, the hill is likely to be backlit and the sky may look harsh.

text.access_note: The Palatine is an archaeological site and may be ticketed or have timed entry, so check the official site before you go.

name: Villa Borghese gardens and Pincio terrace
label: Villa Borghese
camera_source: OpenStreetMap viewpoint 'Balconata del Pincio' (node/649529694).
pin_note: Position from guide/OSM: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Galleria Borghese (museum, 25,490) merged into the gardens spot; its photo rules are not checked. Camera: Pincio terrace over Piazza del Popolo.

text.description:
The Pincio is the terrace on the hill above Piazza del Popolo, and it joins the wider Villa Borghese gardens, a big green area of tree-lined paths on the northern edge of Rome's historic centre. It photographs well because the terrace works as a natural viewing platform. From its edge you look west over the piazza and across the city's rooftops, while the gravel avenues behind you give calm, leafy pictures with a few statues.

The Pincio as you see it was laid out in 1809–14 by Giuseppe Valadier. The paths run out from an obelisk in the middle, put up in 1822 by Pope Pius VII. It is Roman-carved rather than Egyptian, made in the early 2nd century under Hadrian. The Villa Borghese grounds were once about 5 km round and passed to the Italian state in 1902. A pedestrian bridge links the Pincio to the gardens over the road below.

For your phone, treat this as two kinds of picture: one big view from the terrace, and quieter detail shots in the gardens. Start at the terrace edge with the city in front of you, then walk east along the avenues for the trees, the obelisk and the busts that line the paths. Wipe the lens first, keep the phone steady against the balustrade, and take a few frames, because people drift in and out of the view.
text.geographic_location: The Pincio terrace sits on the Pincian Hill on the northern edge of Rome's historic centre, looking down on Piazza del Popolo. The Villa Borghese gardens spread out behind it to the east.
text.directions_text: From Metro line A, Spagna is about 12 minutes on foot from the gardens, which lie to the north of the station. Flaminio, also on Metro line A, is about 12 minutes on foot, with the gardens to the east. From tram 3, Galleria Arte Moderna is about 9 minutes on foot, with the gardens to the south-east. Aldrovandi (tram 19 and tram 3) is also about 9 minutes on foot, with the gardens to the south. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full terrace view and the sky. Switch to the default lens (1x) for people and railings, and the 2x–5x zoom, if your phone has it, to pick out domes and rooftops in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Terrazza del Pincio (central balustrade; move about 20 m south along the terrace for a dome-focused frame). Piazza del Popolo and its twin churches and obelisk in the foreground, with St. Peter's dome on the western horizon and the rooftops of the historic centre beyond. Stand at the Balconata del Pincio viewpoint, on the terrace edge, and face west over Piazza del Popolo.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line. Use the balustrade or a tree branch at the edge of the frame to add depth. In the gardens, line up an avenue so the path leads towards the obelisk or a bust.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the city to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try panorama for the skyline, moving slowly and keeping the phone upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into the evening suits the terrace, because it faces west. Earlier in the day is usually calmer for the garden avenues.

name: Campo de' Fiori
label: Campo de' Fiori
camera_source: Commons cluster, weak (7 photos).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4949430: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Campo de' Fiori' (141 m across).

text.description:
Campo de' Fiori, 'Field of Flowers', is a rectangular square just south of Piazza Navona, on the border of the Parione and Regola districts. The name goes back to the Middle Ages, when this was a meadow. Today it is a lively, slightly jumbled space with no formal architecture, and that is its charm. Market stalls, tall shuttered buildings and café tables all share the same open space, so you get colour and everyday Roman life in a single frame.

A daily vegetable and fish market has been held here since 1869, and it is the best reason to point your phone at the square. The other obvious subject is the monument to Giordano Bruno, put up in 1889 by Ettore Ferrari on the spot where the philosopher was burned in 1600. The statue stands on a base with an inscription, so it works well as a strong central shape against the busy background. The square was also once part of the 'Via papale', the route linking St John Lateran and the Vatican.

For photos, start with a wide view to show the stalls and the surrounding buildings, then move closer for details such as produce, the statue and the small fountain used to keep cut flowers fresh. Keep an eye out for passers-by walking into the frame, and take a few shots rather than one, so you can choose the cleanest.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue or the stall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. Portrait mode works well on fruit and vegetables at close range.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go while the market is running, and check the current days and times before you go. Early in the day it is likely to be quieter, which makes clean wide shots easier.

name: Appian Way (Via Appia Antica)
label: Appian Way
camera_source: PLACED BY CLAUDE (no Commons cluster): on the Via Appia Antica just outside the gate, looking back north at Porta San Sebastiano. Check at the gate. Moved 14 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 70 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/27519297: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Porta San Sebastiano' (43 m across).
notes: Long road: the pin goes at the start near Porta San Sebastiano; much of the park lies south of the central map. Pin not yet placed.

text.description:
Porta San Sebastiano is where the Appian Way leaves Rome's city walls, and it makes a strong first stop for anyone photographing the road. It is the largest and one of the best-preserved gates in the Aurelian Walls. The first version dates from around AD 275, under Emperor Aurelian, and Emperor Honorius reshaped it in AD 401–402. Two sturdy towers flank the arch, and the old brick and marble give you plenty of texture. It was originally called the Porta Appia because it stood where the Appian Way, the 'regina viarum' (queen of the roads), met the city walls. The road itself was begun in 312 BC by Appius Claudius Caecus, ran all the way to Brindisi, and joined the UNESCO World Heritage List in July 2024.

The gate photographs well because it is so solid and so old, and it sits right where the road leaves Rome through the walls. From just outside, you can show the towers, the arch and the line of the road together. Look closer at the jambs, where there is old graffiti and a carved figure of Archangel Michael on the right jamb. Inside the gate is the Museum of the Walls. A phone is ideal here: you can take a wide shot of the whole gate, then step closer or zoom for details. Keep an eye on traffic while you frame your picture, and take your time before moving on.
text.geographic_location: Porta San Sebastiano stands in the Aurelian Walls in Rome, where the Via Appia Antica leaves the city. It is about 1 km north of the Appian Way's start at the walls' edge of the Metro line C station Porta Metronia's southern side.
text.directions_text: From Porta Metronia (Metro line C), the gate is about 1.0 km to the south, about 17 minutes on foot. From Re di Roma (Metro line A), the gate is about 1.4 km to the south-west, about 23 minutes on foot. For trams, such as tram 8, use a journey planner to pick a stop close to the gate. From each station or stop, head towards the gate in the direction given, and look for the large towers of the city wall. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit both towers and the arch in from fairly close, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the 2x–5x zoom, if your phone has it, to pick out stonework and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (on the road in front of the tomb, facing the cobbled Appian Way). The round, battlemented tomb rising beside the ancient basalt paving, with umbrella pines and cypresses framing the road. Stand on the Via Appia Antica just outside the gate and look back towards it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the arch near the centre, with both towers balanced on either side. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. For a second shot, step in close and use the zoom to fill the frame with brick and marble, or crouch low to include the road surface leading to the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate's stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their colour and texture. Avoid ultra-wide close-ups of the towers, which can bend the lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone and fewer people in the shot. Midday sun can flatten the walls and cast hard shadows under the arch.

text.access_note: The road outside the gate is public, but the Museum of the Walls inside the gate may have its own ticket and opening rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Piazza del Popolo
label: Piazza del Popolo
camera_source: OpenStreetMap viewpoint 'Balconata del Pincio' (node/649529694).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/318583: 'Obelisco Flaminio', the best-known feature inside 'Piazza del Popolo' (249 m across).

text.description: Piazza del Popolo is a big oval square at the northern entrance to Rome's historic centre. It photographs well because everything is arranged around a centre line: an Egyptian obelisk in the middle, matching curved walls on each side, and the twin churches of Santa Maria dei Miracoli and Santa Maria in Montesanto at the southern end, where three straight streets (the "trident") fan out into the city. The obelisk is about 24 m high, or 36 m with its plinth. It was brought to Rome in 1 BC and put up here in 1589. Giuseppe Valadier shaped the square as you see it between 1811 and 1822. He also linked it to the Pincio hill above, so you can look down over the whole layout from the terrace. The square was once the first sight of Rome for travellers arriving from the north. Fountains with Neptune and the goddess Roma sit on its two sides, and lions surround the obelisk. For a phone photo, the symmetry does most of the work. Keep the obelisk on the centre line, use the gridlines to keep the verticals straight, and let the curved walls lead the eye inwards. Go for a wide view from above, then a tighter one of the churches or fountains.
text.geographic_location: Piazza del Popolo is in the north of Rome's historic centre, just inside the Porta del Popolo gate in the old Aurelian Walls. The square is about 249 m across, with the Obelisco Flaminio inside it, and the Pincio hill rises on its eastern side.

From the Flaminio (MA) tram stop (tram 2), it also lies to the south, about 3 minutes on foot. From Spagna (Metro line A), head north-west for about 13 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) from the terrace to take in the whole oval. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view. Use 2x-3x zoom to pick out the obelisk, the churches or a fountain without walking closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Terrazza del Pincio (central balustrade, above the piazza (Piazzale Napoleone I)). The oval of the square below with the central obelisk and twin churches, with St Peter's dome on the skyline beyond the rooftops. Lean on the stonework to hold the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the obelisk in the middle of the frame and let the two curved walls make a symmetrical shape around it. Turn on gridlines and line up the buildings with the vertical lines. At the end of your arc, include a little of the balustrade in the foreground to add depth. For a second shot, zoom towards the left (south) to isolate the twin churches.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the obelisk or the sunlit stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. Try panorama mode for a sweep across the oval, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is a good bet, as the sun is behind you and lights the square from the east. At sunset you will be shooting towards the glow, so expect strong contrast; tap on the sky and lower the exposure if you want a silhouette.

text.description:
The Baths of Caracalla are the huge brick ruins of what was once a vast public bathing complex in the south of Rome. It was the city's second largest, after the Baths of Diocletian. It was probably built between AD 212 and 216/217 and inaugurated in AD 216. It stayed in use until the 530s, and after the siege of Rome in 537 cut the water supply, it was abandoned. Later centuries used it as a quarry for stone and decoration, so what you see today is the bare structure rather than the finished marble interiors.

It photographs well because of the scale. Tall, broken walls and big arched openings make strong shapes against the sky, and the warm brick has plenty of texture. It is hard to judge size from a distance, so try to include a person or a doorway for scale. The baths could hold about 1,600 bathers at once, and 6,000 to 8,000 a day is thought to be the daily total. That helps to explain the size of the walls.

On a phone, start wide to take in the whole mass, then move closer for details such as arch edges and brick patterns. Walk a few steps between shots, because the ruins change a lot with your angle. Keep your phone level, using the gridlines, so the tall walls do not lean. Entry rules and routes inside the site can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Baths of Caracalla lie in the south of central Rome, south-east of the Circo Massimo Metro station (Metro line B) and the Aventino/Circo Massimo tram stop.
text.directions_text: From Circo Massimo (Metro line B), the baths are to the south-east, about 8 minutes on foot. The tram stop Aventino/Circo Massimo (tram 3 and tram 8) is also to the south-east, about 9 minutes on foot. From Porta Metronia (Metro line C), walk west for about 14 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m south of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the big walls and arches, especially if you are close to them. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of a single section. Use 2x-3x, if your phone has it, to pick out brickwork and the tops of the arches without walking closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m south of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put a wall or an arch in the foreground and let the larger ruins rise behind it. Switch on the gridlines and line up the vertical edges so the walls look straight. Keep a person or an open doorway in the frame, to show how big the structure is.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white and the bricks keep their colour. If you are shooting upwards and the walls look dark, tap on a shadowed wall and bring the exposure back up.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the brick. Midday sun can be harsh and make deep shadows inside the arches.

text.access_note: The baths are a tourist attraction, so entry may be ticketed or restricted: check the official site before you go.

name: Trajan's Column and the Imperial Forums
label: Trajan's Column
camera_source: Third-largest Commons cluster (12 photos) chosen: the two larger ones are inside Trajan's Markets. Moved 4 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 85 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3376015: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Trajan's Column' (11 m across).
notes: Merged with Via dei Fori Imperiali and Trajan's Market (one walk, one view).

text.description:
Trajan's Column is a tall marble column in the middle of the Imperial Forums, the string of ancient public squares that sit just north of the Roman Forum. It was dedicated on 12 May 113 AD to celebrate Emperor Trajan's victory in the Dacian Wars. The column stands about 30 metres high, or 35 metres with its pedestal. A carved ribbon about 190 metres long winds around the shaft 23 times, showing 155 scenes and more than 2,600 figures. Trajan himself appears 58 times. On top, a bronze figure of Saint Peter was placed in 1587, replacing the emperor's statue that vanished in the Middle Ages.

It photographs well because it is one clear, tall, upright shape with a lot of texture, set among broken ancient walls and columns. That gives you a simple subject with plenty of context around it. The Imperial Forums were built between 46 BC and 113 AD, and the modern road, Via dei Fori Imperiali, now cuts through the middle of the site. Trajan's Markets, the curved brick complex built into the hillside nearby, can also work as a backdrop.

Hold the phone upright, use the gridlines to keep the shaft straight, and take one wide shot for context and one zoomed shot for the carved detail.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Rome, in the Imperial Forums area, just north of the Roman Forum, at about 41.8958° N, 12.4843° E.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is the tram 8 stop 'Venezia', about 279 m away, with the column to the east of the stop. That is about 5 minutes on foot. From the Metro line C station 'Colosseo – Fori Imperiali' the column is about 678 m to the north-west, about 11 minutes on foot. From the Metro line B station 'Cavour' it is about 768 m to the west, about 12 minutes on foot. The tram 8 stop 'Arenula/Cairoli' is about 755 m away, with the column to the east, about 12 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start on the default lens (1x) for the whole column with some of the ruins around it. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the spiral carvings and the figure at the top. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground ruins, and keep the column near the centre so it does not lean or stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Via dei Fori Imperiali (north sidewalk, across from the Victor Emmanuel II Monument, near the Piazza Venezia end). The column rising directly over the forum ruins, with the Basilica Ulpia and Trajan's Market beside it. From here the column is the main vertical in the frame, with the ancient remains of the forums in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright (portrait) and use the gridlines to line the shaft up with a vertical line. Put the column slightly off-centre and let some of the ancient walls fill the bottom of the frame. For a second shot, zoom in on the top third of the column, where the sculpted band and the statue show well.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the column to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down a little so the pale marble keeps its detail and the sky stays blue. Take a few frames in a row, as people often walk through the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset usually gives softer light on the marble and fewer people. At midday the column can look flat and the sky washed out.

text.access_note: Please check the official site for current access details before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The column and the surrounding ruins can be seen and photographed from public viewpoints near Via dei Fori Imperiali.
At about 85 m away, the default lens (1x) on most phones can fit most of the column's height in a portrait-orientation frame.
Early morning or the hour before sunset usually gives softer light and fewer crowds than midday.
Pale marble can lose detail in bright light, so lowering the exposure slider helps.

name: Piazza Venezia and the Vittoriano
label: Vittoriano
camera_source: Commons cluster (159 photos).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/713360712: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Piazza Venezia' (207 m across).
notes: Merged. The Vittoriano's rooftop terrace is also a viewpoint (not yet placed).

text.description:
Piazza Venezia is the busy crossroads at the heart of Rome, where the Via del Corso and the Via dei Fori Imperiali meet at the foot of the Capitoline Hill. On one side stands the Monument to Vittorio Emanuele II, first king of Italy, also called the Altare della Patria or Vittoriano. It holds Italy's Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The square takes its name from the Palazzo Venezia, built by the Venetian cardinal Pietro Barbo, who later became Pope Paul II, next to the church of Saint Mark. It once served as the embassy of the Republic of Venice.

For a phone photo, the appeal is simple. The monument is a huge pale mass that fills the view, and the open square in front gives you room to step back and fit it in. Rome's traffic also adds movement to the foreground. The square has a long history as a gathering place. Mussolini gave speeches here to crowds in the 1920s-1940s, and in 2009 Metro C works uncovered remains of Hadrian's Athenaeum under the middle of the square.

The phone icon on the map is about 170 m south of the subject. From there you can take in the whole monument without tilting the phone steeply upwards, which keeps the columns and corners straight. Keep an eye on traffic and pavements, and take your time rather than stepping into the road for a better angle.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Rome, at the foot of the Capitoline Hill, where the Via del Corso meets the Via dei Fori Imperiali. The Vittoriano stands on one side of the square. The square is named after the nearby Palazzo Venezia.
text.directions_text: The easiest way is tram 8 to the Venezia stop. From there the subject is to the north-east, about 3 minutes on foot. Tram 8 also stops at Arenula/Cairoli, about 10 minutes on foot from the subject, which is again to the north-east. From Metro line C, get off at Colosseo – Fori Imperiali and walk north-west; it is about 13 minutes on foot. From Metro line B, Cavour is about 15 minutes on foot, towards the west. The phone icon on the map is about 170 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand, which should fit the whole monument. If you move much closer, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use 2x or 3x zoom, if your phone has it, to pick out the sculptures and the top of the monument.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 170 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the monument centred, with the vertical lines of the columns running parallel to the grid. Include some of the square or the pavement in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For a second shot, zoom in on the sculptures and the top of the monument.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the monument to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white marble keeps its detail against a bright sky. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone against a railing, a wall or both elbows to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. After dark, use night mode.

text.access_note: Check the official site for opening and access details.

name: Capitoline Hill (Piazza del Campidoglio)
label: Capitoline Hill
camera_source: Commons cluster (157 photos) in the piazza, used instead of the OSM Terrazza Caffarelli viewpoint, which looks out over the city, not at the piazza.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23055100: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Capitol Square' (123 m across).
notes: 'capitoline hill' alone (213,100) is not used: Google appears to merge it with Capitol Hill in Washington. Camera: Terrazza Caffarelli (OSM viewpoint).

text.description: Piazza del Campidoglio is the square on top of the Capitoline Hill, and it is one of the tidiest, most photogenic spaces in Rome. Michelangelo designed it in the 16th century for Pope Paul III, who wanted a showpiece for the visit of Emperor Charles V, expected in 1538. Three palaces frame the square: the Palazzo Senatorio, which is Rome's city hall, and the Palazzo dei Conservatori and Palazzo Nuovo, which together house the Capitoline Museums. The two side palaces mirror one another, so the whole scene feels balanced and symmetrical. Michelangelo's oval design for the paving, with a twelve-pointed star at its centre, dates from 1546. In the middle stands the equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius. It is a copy, because the original is now kept inside the Capitoline Museums. For a phone photo, the symmetry and the patterned pavement are the main draw. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the palace walls stay straight. Step back to fit the buildings and the star pattern into one frame, then move closer for the statue against the sky. People are often in the square, so a little patience helps if you want a clear foreground. The square itself is a public space where you can wander and shoot freely.
text.geographic_location: The piazza sits on top of the Capitoline Hill in central Rome, between the Roman Forum and the Campus Martius. It is in front of Rome's city hall and the Capitoline Museums.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is tram 8 at Venezia, about 4 minutes on foot, with the piazza to the south-east of the stop. From Metro line C, Colosseo – Fori Imperiali is about 10 minutes on foot, and the piazza lies to the west. From Metro line B, Colosseo (also served by tram 3 and tram 8) is about 13 minutes on foot, again with the piazza to the west. Tram 8 at Arenula/Cairoli is also about 10 minutes on foot, with the piazza to the east. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the palaces and the paving together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use 2x or 3x zoom for the statue and the façade details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here you can fit the central area of the piazza and the buildings around it into one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the gridlines on and line up the palace edges with the vertical lines so the buildings don't lean. Keep the star-patterned pavement low in the frame as a leading pattern. For the statue, move closer and put it against the sky or the plain façade behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or a pale wall, then lower the exposure slider a little so the stone keeps its colour. If you use the ultra-wide, keep your phone level to avoid stretched edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stonework and fewer people in the square. Midday sun can be harsh and flat.

text.access_note: The piazza is a public square, so you can wander and take photos there freely.

label: St John Lateran
camera_source: Commons cluster (23 photos, mostly one photographer's series): weak, check at the gate. Moved 68 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 95 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/36444: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilica of Saint John Lateran' (209 m across).
notes: The common name 'st john lateran' was not measured, so this figure may be low.

text.description:
St John Lateran is the cathedral of Rome. It is also the seat of the pope as Bishop of Rome. It was founded in 324, making it the oldest public church in the city and the oldest basilica in the Western world. It was rebuilt in the late 16th century under Pope Sixtus V, and the big façade was completed in 1735 under Clement XII.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is scale and order. The façade is a broad, formal frontage with a long Latin inscription naming Clement XII and the dedication to Christ the Saviour. That makes a good detail shot as well as a wide one. Because the building is so large, you will rarely fit all of it in at 1x unless you stand well back.

Begin with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole frontage, then switch to 2x or more for the inscription and architectural details. Keep your phone upright and check the gridlines so the vertical lines stay straight. Wait a moment for people to move out of the foreground, or include them to show the scale. It is a working church, so be considerate when photographing near entrances.
text.geographic_location: St John Lateran stands next to the Lateran Palace, close to San Giovanni Metro station (Metro line A and Metro line C). The Vatican is roughly four kilometres to the north-west.
text.directions_text: From San Giovanni (Metro line A or Metro line C), head west; it is about 6 minutes on foot. From the tram 3 and tram 8 stop Porta S. Giovanni/Carlo Felice, walk west for about 5 minutes. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole façade, then use 1x for a calmer, less stretched view. Use 2x–5x, depending on your phone, for the Latin inscription and architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza di San Giovanni in Laterano (in front of the main facade, facing west). The full travertine facade with its row of statues, with the church's square and the Lateran Palace framing the scene, and the obelisk in the square. Walk a little each way to find a clear view with fewer obstructions.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the phone upright and level, and turn on gridlines to keep the vertical edges straight. At 0.5x, keep the façade away from the edges of the frame to limit stretching. For a second shot, go to 2x and frame the inscription and the top of the façade, leaving some sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Try panorama only if you cannot step back far enough, and hold the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters pale stone, and arriving early may mean fewer people in the foreground.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go for access, visiting times and dress code.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters pale stone.
There may be fewer people in the foreground early in the day.
The façade is too large to fit fully in a 1x frame unless you stand well back.
Ultra-wide shots can stretch objects near the edge of the frame.
